subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 10 periods = 400 minutes
Total: 10 periods · 6h 40min

periods.activity_title: Who Lives Near Plants? — A Recognition Walk
periods.textbook_anchor: Plants and Animals Live Together — Students discuss which animals from the textbook illustration they have seen before and describe their size using hands and arms (p. 64)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 63 visual spread of twelve animals

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens Textbook p. 63 and invites students to look at the full spread of twelve animals quietly. Ask: which of these have you actually seen — near your home, in a garden, on a tree, under a stone? Students call out names freely; the teacher lists them on the board without sorting yet.

Students open Textbook p. 64 and take turns describing where and how they saw one of the animals. The teacher prompts: Was it on a leaf, in the soil, on a branch, flying? After each description, the class uses fingers, hands, and arms to show how small or big that animal is — a quick, whole-body sizing exercise.

Guided discussion: the teacher points to the board list and asks which of these animals live underground. Students reason aloud, drawing on the textbook image. The teacher introduces the 'Do you know?' panel on the same page and reads two or three examples together (owls nesting in tree hollows, tailorbirds stitching leaves, caterpillars eating leaves) to model how animals use plants for food, shelter, and rearing young.

Closing circle: each student shares one animal from the page and one way it uses a plant, in a single sentence. The teacher collects a few and notes any animals students have not yet seen in their own surroundings, framing this as something to look out for on the way home.

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe, using personal observation, how familiar animals relate to plants in their immediate environment.
periods.section_context: Frog, tailorbird, elephants, squirrels, ants, caterpillar, butterfly, woodpecker, moth, barbet, stink bug, earthworms; animal use of plants for food, shelter, and nesting from the 'Do you know?' panel.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Which of these animals would your grandmother or an elder in your family know well — and what would they say about it?' This draws out local and intergenerational knowledge naturally. Group students so that those who have seen fewer animals are seated beside those who have seen more, so descriptions travel across experience levels.

periods.activity_title: Why Animals Choose Plants — A Reasoning Discussion
periods.textbook_anchor: Plants and Animals Live Together — Students investigate why animals choose to live near plants (p. 64)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 63 visual spread (reference during discussion)

time_bands.activity: The teacher poses the central question from Textbook p. 64: 'Why do these animals choose to live near plants?' Students think quietly for a moment, then share initial guesses freely. The teacher records key words on the board without evaluating them — food, hide, sleep, nest, water, safe — whatever students offer.

The class revisits the 'Do you know?' panel. The teacher reads one example at a time (camels and leaves; owls in hollow trees; crows and twigs; sunbirds and nectar; bats on branches; leopards resting on branches) and after each, students identify which need is being met — food, shelter, or raising young. The teacher draws a simple three-column chart on the board: Food | Shelter | Raising Young, and students call out which column each animal belongs in.

Pair talk: each pair chooses one animal from the board list and agrees on which plant part that animal depends on most and why. Pairs share back to the class. The teacher asks: 'Can the animal survive if that plant part were gone?' to deepen reasoning.

Students write two sentences in their notebooks: one naming an animal and the plant it depends on, and one giving the reason for that dependence. The teacher circulates and reads a few aloud to close the unit.

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain, using reasoning from evidence, why animals depend on plants to meet their basic needs.
periods.section_context: Animal needs (food, shelter, rearing young) fulfilled by plants; camels, owls, crows, sunbirds, bats, leopards, caterpillars, monkeys, butterflies in relation to specific plant parts.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt: 'If all the trees in your neighbourhood were cut down, which animals do you think would leave first, and why?' This keeps reasoning local and concrete. Allow students who name different animals from their own region — a palm tree, a neem, a mango — to anchor their examples there.

periods.activity_title: Soil Investigation — Look, Feel, and Smell
periods.textbook_anchor: Life in the Soil — Students pick up soil near a plant and investigate its look, feel, moisture, and smell, noting any leaves or insects found (p. 64)
materials: Small trowels or sticks for collecting soil (one per group)
A patch of soil near the school building or a potted plant
Sheets of newspaper or trays to place soil on

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the investigation prompt from Textbook p. 64 aloud with the class. Students are told they will each collect a small amount of soil from near the school plant or pot and bring it back to their desks on a newspaper sheet. The teacher demonstrates the safe amount to pick up — a loose palmful — and reminds students to use hands gently.

In small groups, students collect their soil samples and return to their seats. Each student examines the soil using the guiding words from the textbook: Is it dry, damp, rough, smooth, hard, or grainy? They note the colour. They look carefully for any leaves, roots, or insects. Each student records observations in their notebook using words or simple sketches.

Students smell the soil — the teacher encourages them to close their eyes and notice the smell. Is it earthy, sweet, sharp? The teacher asks: 'Did you find anything living in the soil?' Students share findings across groups. The teacher introduces the concept from Textbook p. 64: soil is made from broken rock fragments, old leaves, roots, stems, and living and dead animals — a living system, not just dirt.

Students write two observations in their notebooks: one describing what they saw in the soil and one describing what they smelled or felt. The teacher asks: 'Do you think soil from a bare patch with no plants nearby would feel and smell the same?' Students respond briefly in pairs before the unit closes.

periods.implied_lo: Students can carry out a sensory investigation of a natural material and record observable properties using descriptive language.
periods.section_context: Soil near a plant; properties: colour, texture (rough, smooth, hard, grainy), moisture (dry, damp), smell; contents: leaves, roots, insects found in soil.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Has anyone at home — a grandparent or a farmer relative — ever smelled soil before planting and said something about it? What did they say?' This invites traditional knowledge about soil quality into the conversation without making it a separate topic. Keep the collection phase unhurried so students actually engage with what they find.

periods.activity_title: Soil Away from Plants — Comparing Two Samples
periods.textbook_anchor: Life in the Soil — Students compare soil from under a plant and soil away from plants (p. 64)
materials: Two newspaper sheets or trays per group — one labelled 'Near plant', one labelled 'Away from plant'

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens Textbook p. 64 and reminds students of the soil investigation they have already completed. Today they will collect a second sample — from a patch of ground that has no plant growing on or near it — and compare it with what they remember or recorded before. The teacher explains how to label the two newspaper sheets clearly.

In groups, students collect the second soil sample and lay it alongside the first (either a new sample from near the plant or their notes from the earlier investigation). They examine both: colour comparison, texture comparison, moisture comparison, smell comparison, and whether each contains visible living things. Students record findings in a simple two-column layout in their notebooks: Near plant | Away from plant.

Groups share their comparisons. The teacher builds a class chart on the board with the same two-column structure and populates it from student reports. The teacher then asks: 'What might explain the differences you noticed?' Students reason about roots, dead leaves, and animals adding material to the soil near plants — connecting observations to the textbook's explanation of soil composition.

Closing discussion: the teacher asks which sample they think earthworms and ants would prefer, and why. Students respond using evidence from their own samples. A brief written sentence in notebooks closes the unit: 'Soil near a plant is different from soil away from plants because…'

periods.implied_lo: Students can compare two specimens of the same material from different locations and use observed differences to reason about why living things are found in one location rather than another.
periods.section_context: Soil near a plant compared with soil away from plants; properties compared: colour, texture, moisture, smell, presence of living things (ants, earthworms, insects).
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt: 'Has anyone grown something at home in a pot or in the ground? How did that soil look compared with soil from a footpath?' This local-home connection makes the comparison concrete. If two outdoor patches are not available, a pot of soil versus a tray of dry swept-up dirt from the corridor works equally well.

periods.activity_title: Animals Near My Plant Friend — Observation Table
periods.textbook_anchor: Life in the Soil — Students stand near their plant friend, spot animals, describe them in words, and fill in the observation table (p. 66)
materials: Access to a school plant or a corner of the school garden

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens Textbook p. 66 and reads the activity prompt with the class. Students are told they will stand quietly near the school plant for a short, unhurried observation period — no running, no collecting animals, just watching. The teacher models how to look: at the soil surface, on stems, under leaves, in the air nearby.

Students move to the plant area in small quiet groups (staggered if space is limited) and observe without disturbing the plant. They note every animal they spot — on the leaves, in the soil, flying near, on the bark. They use the reference pictures on Textbook p. 66 if they cannot name an animal. Each student records at least two animals in their notebook: name or description, where they saw it (leaf, soil, stem, air), and one word about what it was doing.

Back at their seats, students transfer their notes into the structured table from Textbook p. 66: animal name or description, location on or near the plant, behaviour observed. The teacher circulates and encourages precise language: 'not just under the plant — under which part, and doing what?'

A brief share-out: each group names one animal they spotted that another group might have missed. The teacher asks: 'Of all the animals you saw, which one surprised you most, and what do you think it was doing near the plant?' This closes the observation on a reflective note.

periods.implied_lo: Students can conduct a structured outdoor observation, record findings in a table, and describe the position and behaviour of living things using precise language.
periods.section_context: Animals observed near a school plant: insects, ants, birds, beetles, or whatever is locally present; location on plant (leaf, stem, soil, bark, air); behaviour noted; reference to textbook animal pictures.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Open question for the share-out: 'Did you notice any animal doing something that seemed helpful to the plant — or harmful to it?' Keep the outdoor phase genuinely unhurried so students observe rather than race to fill the table.

periods.activity_title: Monsoon and New Life — Seasonal Change Discussion
periods.textbook_anchor: Life in the Soil — Students discuss where new plants and animals come from in the monsoon and why they were not visible earlier (p. 66)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens Textbook p. 66 and reads the discussion prompt aloud: 'In the monsoons, you may find many more plants and animals around. Where did these new plants and animals come from? Why could you not see them earlier?' Students think quietly, then share initial ideas freely. The teacher lists key student ideas on the board: seeds, rain, eggs, underground, hidden.

The teacher facilitates a guided discussion moving through three questions: (1) Where were the seeds before the rains came? (2) Where were the earthworms and millipedes? (3) What does rain do that makes it possible for them to appear? Students connect the earlier soil investigation — moisture, living things in soil — to the seasonal appearance of new animals and plants.

Students share personal monsoon memories: frogs appearing, grass growing overnight, ants forming trails, mushrooms on tree trunks. The teacher asks: 'Have elders at home told you any signs that the monsoon is coming — before the rain even falls?' This draws in seasonal and observational knowledge held in families. The teacher notes examples on the board.

Students write two sentences in their notebooks: one explaining where the new animals come from in the monsoon and one saying what conditions make this possible. A closing question from the teacher: 'If the monsoon did not come one year, what might happen to the animals near our plant friend?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain how seasonal change in one environmental condition (rainfall) triggers visible change in the number and variety of plants and animals in a familiar place.
periods.section_context: Monsoon season; new plants and animals appearing after rain; earthworms and millipedes emerging; seeds germinating; soil moisture as a trigger; seasonal and elder-held knowledge of monsoon signs.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt: 'Has anyone seen earthworms or frogs appear suddenly after heavy rain? Where do you think they come from?' If students mention specific local signs their families use to predict rain (behaviour of ants, certain bird calls, the smell of soil), validate and build on these as genuine observations.

periods.activity_title: Listening for Birds — Sound Localisation Investigation
periods.textbook_anchor: Life in the Soil — Students listen for bird sounds, cup their ears to localise direction, and record bird sounds heard at different times (p. 68)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 68 bird sound recording table

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens Textbook p. 68 and reads the activity prompt with the class. Students are told they will first try the investigation indoors — closing eyes and listening — then move outside briefly if the school allows. The teacher demonstrates cupping both hands behind the ears (like satellite dishes) and turning the head slowly toward a sound source to find its direction.

Indoors: students close their eyes for a full, unhurried silence. The teacher quietly taps on different parts of the room (far wall, window, door) and asks students to point toward the sound without opening their eyes. Then students cup their ears and repeat — do they find the direction more easily? They discuss the difference as a class.

Students open Textbook p. 68 and begin filling in the sound recording table with any bird sounds they can recall or currently hear (through a window, during outdoor time earlier in the day). For each bird they write: the name if known, a description of the sound (shrill, soft, repeated, melodic), and the time of day they normally hear it — early morning, afternoon, or evening. The teacher asks: 'What if you hear no birds at all — what might that tell us?'

Class discussion: do students hear more bird sounds at a particular time of day? The teacher maps responses on the board (early morning | afternoon | evening) as a tally. Students reason about why birds might call more at certain times. A closing sentence in notebooks: one bird sound the student recognises, described in their own words.

periods.implied_lo: Students can design and carry out a simple sensory investigation — using their ears and body position — to collect and record data about sounds in their environment.
periods.section_context: Bird sounds heard at different times of day (early morning, afternoon, evening); ear-cupping technique for sound localisation; names or descriptions of local bird calls; reasons for absence of bird sounds.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Does anyone know a bird call that their family member taught them to recognise — maybe a bird that signals rain, or one that comes at harvest time?' This surfaces intergenerational nature knowledge without labelling it. If the school is in a quiet urban setting with few birds, treat the absence of sound as data and discuss what that might mean for the ecosystem.

periods.activity_title: Describing My Observations — Animal and Plant Drawing with Dots
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students draw their plant friend and use coloured dots to mark where they spotted animals, birds, or insects (p. 71)
materials: At least three different coloured pencils or crayons per student
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 71 drawing and dot-marking prompt

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens Textbook p. 71 and explains the task: students will draw their plant friend — the plant they have been observing — and then place small coloured dots on the drawing to mark every spot where they saw an animal, bird, or insect. The teacher demonstrates on the board: a rough plant outline with a dot on a leaf, a dot in the soil, a dot near the stem. Each colour stands for a different kind of animal (e.g., insects: one colour; birds: another; worms: a third).

Students draw their plant from memory or from their observation notes. The drawing does not need to be detailed — the structure (roots, stem, leaves, branches) is what matters. Once the outline is done, students add coloured dots at every location where they observed a living creature during the chapter's activities. Beside or below the drawing, they write a brief key: what each colour represents.

Students look at a partner's drawing and describe one similarity and one difference between the two: 'You have a dot on the bark but I don't — what did you see there?' The teacher circulates and asks students to explain a dot they placed: what was there, what was it doing, and why was it at that spot on the plant?

The teacher closes with a whole-class question: 'Looking at all your drawings together, which part of the plant seemed to have the most animal visitors?' Students respond briefly. The drawings are kept in their notebooks for personal reference.

periods.implied_lo: Students can represent their field observations visually and spatially, using a drawing with a symbolic key to communicate where and what they observed.
periods.section_context: Plant friend drawing; coloured dot placement marking animal, bird, insect locations on the plant; dot key by animal type; plant parts (leaves, stem, bark, roots, soil, branches) as location markers.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt during the drawing phase: 'Do you want to add anything that a family member or someone from your neighbourhood told you lives in or around this kind of plant — even if you did not see it yourself?' This allows cultural and intergenerational knowledge to enter the drawing as a note or a special mark. Resist tidying up students' drawings — rough, honest plant sketches with confident dots are more informative than neat but invented ones.

periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students fill in a table describing the shape, size, colour, and reasons for presence of two animals observed near or on plants (p. 70)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens Textbook p. 70 and reads the write task prompt with the class. Students are reminded that they have been observing animals near plants across several activities — the soil investigation, the outdoor observation, and their drawings. Now they will write carefully about two animals they actually saw, using the structured table on Textbook p. 70: name, shape, size, colours, reason for being near the plant, and any other interesting thing they noticed.

Students work individually to fill in the table for their two chosen animals. The teacher prompts precise description: 'Don't write big or small — use your hands to show and then find a word. Don't write it was near the plant — say whether it was on a leaf, in the soil, on the bark, or flying close.' The teacher circulates and reads entries, asking follow-up questions to deepen descriptions.

Pairs swap notebooks and read each other's entries. The partner asks one clarifying question: 'How did you know it was doing that?' or 'What colour exactly?' Students add or refine one detail in their own entry after the swap. The teacher asks two or three students to read out their entries to the class.

The teacher closes with the discussion questions from Textbook p. 70: 'Which animals, birds, and insects did you notice around plants? How do animals, birds, and insects rely on plants — and which example was your favourite?' Two or three students respond briefly to close the unit.

periods.implied_lo: Students can record and communicate precise observational descriptions of living things, including physical attributes and inferred reasons for their presence in a habitat.
periods.section_context: Two animals observed near or on plants; attributes described: shape, size, colour; reason for presence near plant (food, shelter, nesting); additional interesting observations; structured table from the reflection section.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students who struggle to recall a specific animal: 'Think back to the dot you placed on your drawing — what did you put there and why?' The dot drawing from the previous activity can serve as a personal memory prompt without requiring that activity to have been formally set. Open question for the share-out: 'Did anyone choose an animal that surprised them — one they didn't expect to find near a plant?'

periods.activity_title: From Soil to Sky — Whole-Chapter Synthesis
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students sequence the stages of a caterpillar's life cycle and discuss what they have learned about how plants and animals live together (p. 71)
materials: Strips of paper (one set per group, pre-cut with one life-cycle stage written on each)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens Textbook p. 71 and introduces the sequencing task: the story of Suma and the caterpillar. The five stages are written on the board in scrambled order — 'Now it was a butterfly', 'The caterpillar formed a cocoon', 'It flew away gently', 'One day it stopped eating', 'It came out of the cocoon'. Students work in small groups with paper strips to arrange the stages in order, consulting each other and, where possible, an elder in the room (another teacher visiting, an older student, or the teacher in role). Groups share their sequence and the class agrees on the correct order.

The teacher uses the life cycle as a bridge back to the whole chapter: the caterpillar ate leaves (food from plants), rested on a branch (shelter from plants), formed a cocoon attached to a stem (nesting on plants), and became a butterfly that drinks nectar (food from plants again). The teacher asks the class to name everything from the chapter that shows plants giving animals food, shelter, or a place to raise young — students call out and the teacher maps these on the board under three headings: Food | Shelter | Raising Young.

The teacher draws a large simple plant outline on the board (roots, stem, leaves, branches). Students come up one at a time and write or draw one animal from the chapter at the part of the plant it uses — earthworm in the roots, ant in the soil, tailorbird on the leaf, woodpecker on the bark, butterfly above the flower. The class builds a collective 'plant and animal community' diagram as a culminating representation of the chapter's core idea.

Reflection circle: the teacher asks three questions in sequence, giving students a moment to think before each answer. (1) 'Of everything we explored in this chapter — soil, sounds, seasons, animals, life cycles — what do you now notice differently when you walk past a plant?' (2) 'If a plant in your neighbourhood were harmed or cut down, which animals would be most affected?' (3) 'What is one thing you would like to find out more about?' Students respond briefly; the teacher notes the final question on the board as 'Questions we still have.'

The teacher closes by reading the chapter's core idea aloud: wherever plants grow, animals live on, around, and underneath them — in the soil, on the branches, in the air nearby. Students repeat it quietly to themselves. The chapter closes on the image of the plant as a home, a pantry, and a nursery for the animals that live with it.

periods.implied_lo: Students can synthesise observations across multiple natural phenomena — soil, seasonal change, animal behaviour, and life cycles — to articulate the interdependence between plants and animals in a shared environment.
periods.section_context: Caterpillar life cycle stages (caterpillar, cocoon, butterfly) sequencing; Suma story from the textbook; whole-chapter synthesis: food, shelter, raising young provided by plants; board diagram of plant and animal community; reflection on what changes in one's own noticing of plants.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: For the sequencing task, invite the teacher or an older student from another class to play the 'elder' role if one is available — the textbook explicitly asks students to consult an elder. Open question for the reflection: 'Before this chapter, when you walked past a plant, what did you see? What do you think you will see now?' This surfaces the change in observation and attention that the chapter has been building.

assessment_items.question_text: You are looking at a tree in your school garden. Which of the following is the best way to find out how many different animals live on or near the tree?

options.label: A
options.text: Ask a friend to name all the animals that live in trees everywhere.

options.label: B
options.text: Count only the animals you can see flying in the air near the tree.

options.label: C
options.text: Read a book about trees and write down every animal mentioned in it.

options.label: D
options.text: Stand quietly near the tree, look at the leaves, bark, soil, and branches, and note every animal you spot.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is B. This item assesses whether students understand that personal, on-site observation of the immediate environment — looking at multiple plant parts — is the method the chapter builds, not book knowledge or second-hand accounts.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe, using personal observation, how familiar animals relate to plants in their immediate environment.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student substitutes second-hand knowledge (asking someone else) for direct observation — a confusion between inquiry and information-gathering.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student treats book knowledge as equivalent to personal observation of their own environment, missing the chapter's core method.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student restricts observation to one location (the air) rather than scanning all plant parts — partial observation rather than structured whole-plant observation.

assessment_items.question_text:
Look at the list below. For each animal, write ONE need — food, shelter, or raising young — that the animal gets from the plant part named.

1. Caterpillar — leaf
2. Owl — hollow in a tree trunk
3. Sunbird — flower
expected_elements: Caterpillar — food (the caterpillar eats the leaf).
Owl — shelter (the owl nests or rests inside the hollow).
Sunbird — food (the sunbird drinks nectar from the flower).
assessment_items.annotation: Award one mark per correct need correctly matched to the animal-plant pair. Accept reasonable synonyms: 'home' for shelter, 'eating' or 'drinking' for food. Regional variation note: if a student names a local equivalent flower-visiting bird instead of sunbird, the response is equally correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain, using reasoning from evidence, why animals depend on plants to meet their basic needs.

competency.competency_text: Identifies needs of plants, birds, and animals, and how they can be supported (water, soil, food, care)

expected_elements: Caterpillar — food: the caterpillar eats the leaf to get energy.
Owl — shelter: the owl uses the hollow trunk to rest or nest safely.
Sunbird — food: the sunbird drinks nectar from the flower.

assessment_items.question_text:
Priya picked up a handful of soil from under a flowering plant in her garden. She noticed it was dark, damp, and smelled strong. She also found two small insects and a piece of old leaf in it.

Name TWO things Priya observed about the soil and explain what each one tells us about the soil.
expected_elements: One observable property named (e.g. dark colour, damp texture, strong smell, or presence of insects or leaf pieces).
A second, different observable property named.

An explanation for at least one property connecting it to what that property suggests about the soil (e.g. damp means it holds water; insects mean living things are present; old leaf means plant material is breaking down).
assessment_items.annotation: Award marks for any two genuine properties from the scenario and a reasonable interpretive statement for at least one. Students need not use technical terms — 'it means the soil has water in it' is acceptable for damp. Do not penalise if the student adds a third property.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can carry out a sensory investigation of a natural material and record observable properties using descriptive language.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: Property 1 named: dark colour / damp / strong smell / presence of insects or leaf matter.
Property 2 named: a different property from the list above.
At least one explanation connecting a property to what it indicates (e.g. damp soil holds water; insects show living things are in the soil; old leaf shows plant material is present).

assessment_items.question_text:
Arun collected soil from under a mango tree and soil from a bare footpath. He noticed that the soil from under the tree was dark and had ants and small insects in it, while the footpath soil was pale and had nothing living in it.

What is the MOST LIKELY reason the soil under the tree has more living things in it?

options.label: A
options.text: The ants moved there because the mango fruits fell nearby, but soil itself is the same everywhere.

options.label: B
options.text: The colour of the soil changes because of the shadow of the tree, and darker soil attracts animals.

options.label: C
options.text: The footpath soil is too hard because people walk on it, and that alone keeps animals away.

options.label: D
options.text: The soil under the tree gets fallen leaves, roots, moisture, and shade from the tree, which living things need.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is B. This item assesses whether students can use their comparison investigation to reason about why plant-adjacent soil supports more life — connecting soil composition (leaves, roots, moisture) to the presence of organisms.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can compare two specimens of the same material from different locations and use observed differences to reason about why living things are found in one location rather than another.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student identifies one real factor (compaction from foot traffic) but treats it as the sole cause, missing the plant-soil relationship entirely.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student partially reasons about one plant product (fruit) but dismisses the broader role of the plant in enriching soil — a partial-cause error.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student confuses correlation (shade makes things look darker) with causation, and invents a mechanism (colour attracting animals) not present in the chapter.

assessment_items.question_text:
Meena stood near her plant friend to observe animals. She wanted to record her observations carefully.

Which of the following would give her the MOST useful information to write in her observation table?

options.label: A
options.text: A large ant was moving quickly across the surface of a leaf.

options.label: B
options.text: I think birds live in this plant because all plants have birds.

options.label: C
options.text: The plant was big and had many leaves.

options.label: D
options.text: There were some animals near the plant.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is A, because it names the animal, its location (on a leaf), and what it was doing (moving quickly) — the three components the observation table requires. Options B and C show vague or irrelevant descriptions; D substitutes assumption for observation.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can conduct a structured outdoor observation, record findings in a table, and describe the position and behaviour of living things using precise language.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes diversity among plants, and birds and animals in their immediate environment (shape, sounds, food habits, growth, habitat)

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student records a vague category ('some animals') without naming, locating, or describing behaviour — they have not yet understood what structured observation requires.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student describes the plant rather than the animals — a focus confusion between the background and the subject of observation.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student substitutes a general assumption ('all plants have birds') for actual observation — replacing evidence with prior belief.

assessment_items.question_text:
After the monsoon rains arrived, Raju noticed that there were suddenly many more earthworms, frogs, and new green plants around the big tree in his village. Before the rains, he had seen none of these.

Why do you think these plants and animals appeared after the rains? Give at least two reasons and explain your thinking.
look_for: The student identifies moisture or water from rain as a key trigger — seeds need water to germinate, animals come out of the soil when it is wet.

The student distinguishes between things that were hidden or dormant (seeds underground, earthworms deep in dry soil) and things that were genuinely absent — showing understanding of seasonal hiding rather than seasonal arrival.

The student connects at least one specific organism (earthworm, frog, or plant) to a specific reason (earthworms come to the surface when soil is wet; seeds germinate in moist soil; frogs breed in standing water).
The student's reasoning is grounded in the natural phenomenon rather than in a vague statement such as 'the rain brought them'.
assessment_items.annotation: A strong response names at least two organisms and gives distinct, organism-specific reasons for their appearance. A weak response gives one general reason for all organisms without distinguishing them. Regional variation note: students may mention locally familiar monsoon organisms (e.g. specific frogs, snails, mushrooms, grass species) — all are valid if the reasoning is sound.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how seasonal change in one environmental condition (rainfall) triggers visible change in the number and variety of plants and animals in a familiar place.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

look_for: Identifies moisture/water from rain as a trigger for at least one organism's appearance.
Shows understanding that seeds, earthworms, or animals were present but hidden or dormant — not newly created by the rain.
Gives organism-specific reasoning for at least two different organisms (e.g. earthworms + plants, or frogs + seeds).
Grounds the explanation in the natural environment rather than in a vague claim that rain 'brings' animals from elsewhere.

assessment_items.question_text:
Sona closed her eyes and listened for birds near her school garden. She heard a loud, sharp call from her left. She then cupped her hands behind her ears and pointed her face to the left.

(a) Why did Sona cup her hands behind her ears?
(b) She heard more bird sounds in the early morning than in the afternoon. Write one possible reason for this.
expected_elements: (a) Cupping the hands helps collect more sound and makes it easier to tell which direction a sound is coming from — the sound becomes louder or clearer.

(b) Any one reasonable explanation: birds are more active in the morning (feeding, calling to each other); afternoon heat may make birds rest quietly; fewer other sounds compete with bird calls in the morning.
assessment_items.annotation: For (a), accept any phrasing that captures sound collection or direction-finding — the student need not use technical vocabulary. For (b), accept any ecologically plausible reason; regional variation note: students in areas with specific dawn-calling species may name those birds, which is correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can design and carry out a simple sensory investigation — using their ears and body position — to collect and record data about sounds in their environment.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: (a) Cupping hands behind ears collects sound and helps locate its direction — the sound becomes louder or clearer.
(b) One plausible reason: birds call more in the morning because they are active and feeding; or afternoon heat reduces activity; or morning is quieter so bird calls carry further.

assessment_items.task: Draw a plant — any plant you have seen near your home or school. On your drawing, place small coloured dots to show where you have seen or expect to see living creatures (animals, birds, insects, or worms). Make a key below your drawing to show what each colour means.
assessment_items.scaffold: Your drawing can be simple — roots, a stem, leaves, and branches are enough. Choose at least three different colours. For each colour, write in the key: the colour, the creature it stands for, and the part of the plant where you placed it. You may add a short note next to one dot saying what the creature was doing there.
format_of_output: A plant drawing with dots placed at observation locations
A colour key naming each creature and the plant part it was found on
An optional note on one dot describing the creature's behaviour or reason for being there
assessment_items.annotation: Assess on: (1) whether the plant has recognisable parts used as location markers; (2) whether dots are placed at meaningful locations (not scattered randomly); (3) whether the key connects each colour to a named or described creature. Do not assess drawing quality. Regional variation note: any plant and any locally familiar creatures are fully correct — the task is spatial and communicative, not a test of species names.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can represent their field observations visually and spatially, using a drawing with a symbolic key to communicate where and what they observed.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can translate observation into a spatial-visual representation with a symbolic coding system, showing that they understand where on a plant different animals are found and can communicate that spatially.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold structures the task into three achievable steps: draw the plant, place dots, write the key. Students who struggle with drawing should be encouraged to make a schematic (box for soil, line for stem, triangle for leaves) — the dot placement and key are the core outcomes.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: dots placed at ecologically meaningful locations (ants in soil, butterfly near flowers, bird on branch), key clearly names creature and location, optional note shows reasoning. Weak: dots scattered without reference to plant parts, key is absent or lists colours without creatures.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who have not observed plants outdoors may use the textbook's twelve-animal image as a reference for dot placement. Students who cannot write the key may dictate it to the teacher or draw small creature sketches instead of words.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Drawing with a symbolic key is the exact mode the textbook prescribes for this reflection task; it assesses spatial reasoning and communication without requiring extended writing.

assessment_items.task: Choose two animals you have seen near or on a plant. For each animal, write its name (or describe it if you do not know its name), describe its shape and colour, and give one reason why you think it was near that plant — was it looking for food, shelter, or something else?
assessment_items.scaffold:
Use this format for each animal:
Animal 1: Name or description — Shape — Colour — Reason for being near the plant — One interesting thing I noticed
Animal 2: Name or description — Shape — Colour — Reason for being near the plant — One interesting thing I noticed
format_of_output: Two filled-in entries in the scaffold format, one per animal
A reason for presence near the plant for each animal
At least one interesting observation for each animal
assessment_items.annotation: Assess on: (1) whether physical attributes (shape, colour) are described with at least some specificity; (2) whether the reason for presence connects to a genuine plant-animal relationship (food, shelter, nesting); (3) whether the 'interesting thing' reflects actual observation rather than a guess. Do not penalise for unknown species names — a clear description ('a small green insect with a pointed nose') is fully acceptable. Regional variation note: any locally observed animal near any plant is correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can record and communicate precise observational descriptions of living things, including physical attributes and inferred reasons for their presence in a habitat.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes diversity among plants, and birds and animals in their immediate environment (shape, sounds, food habits, growth, habitat)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can move from observation to description — translating what they saw into specific physical attributes and an inferred ecological reason, using the chapter's conceptual framework (food, shelter, raising young).
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold guides students through attribute-by-attribute description. Teachers should accept any sequence — students who write the interesting observation first and the colour second are demonstrating the same competency.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: specific shape and colour details, a reason that names a specific plant part (eating the leaf, hiding under bark), an interesting observation that shows the student watched the animal rather than guessed. Weak: vague attributes ('it was small and brown'), a reason with no plant connection ('it was there because it wanted to'), no interesting observation.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who did not observe animals directly may describe animals from the textbook's twelve-animal spread, provided they give a reason rooted in the chapter's content. Students who cannot write may draw the two animals with labels and explain verbally.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Structured written description using a two-entry scaffold
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The scaffold mirrors the textbook's own observation table format, making the task a direct extension of the activity students completed — reducing the cognitive overhead of organising a free-form response.

assessment_items.question_text:
The stages of a caterpillar's life are listed below, but they are not in the right order:

— Now it was a butterfly.
— The caterpillar formed a cocoon.
— It flew away gently.
— One day it stopped eating.
— It came out of the cocoon.

Which of the following shows the CORRECT order of these stages?

options.label: A
options.text: It flew away gently → Now it was a butterfly → It came out of the cocoon → The caterpillar formed a cocoon → One day it stopped eating.

options.label: B
options.text: One day it stopped eating → It came out of the cocoon → The caterpillar formed a cocoon → Now it was a butterfly → It flew away gently.

options.label: C
options.text: One day it stopped eating → The caterpillar formed a cocoon → It came out of the cocoon → Now it was a butterfly → It flew away gently.

options.label: D
options.text: The caterpillar formed a cocoon → One day it stopped eating → It came out of the cocoon → Now it was a butterfly → It flew away gently.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is B. This item assesses whether students can correctly sequence the caterpillar life cycle from the chapter's story of Suma. The cycle runs: stops eating → forms cocoon → comes out of cocoon → is now a butterfly → flies away.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can synthesise observations across multiple natural phenomena — soil, seasonal change, animal behaviour, and life cycles — to articulate the interdependence between plants and animals in a shared environment.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student places cocoon formation before the caterpillar stops eating — confusing the trigger (stopping eating signals the transition) with the cocoon stage that follows it.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student places emergence from the cocoon before the cocoon is formed — a logical reversal showing that the sequence has not been internalised.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student reverses the entire life cycle, reading the stages backwards — a complete sequence confusion rather than a specific stage error.
